hints: List the atoms on each side first, then check charge. You have $\text{Cl}$, $\text{O}$ and $\text{S}$ to balance, plus an overall ionic charge.
walkthrough:
Track what changes and what stays**
You are told the only products are $\text{ClO}_2$ and $\text{SO}_4^{2-}$ from $\text{ClO}_3^-$ and $\text{SO}_2$. So write the skeleton: $\text{ClO}_3^- + \text{SO}_2 \rightarrow \text{ClO}_2 + \text{SO}_4^{2-}$. Check $\text{Cl}$ and $\text{S}$, they are already one to one.

Balance O and charge together**
Count $\text{O}$: left has $3+2=5$, right has $2+4=6$. Count charge: left has $-1$, right has $-2$. Doubling the $\text{Cl}$ species fixes both at once: $2\text{ClO}_3^- + \text{SO}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{ClO}_2 + \text{SO}_4^{2-}$. Now $\text{O}$ is $8$ on both sides, $\text{Cl}$ is $2$, $\text{S}$ is $1$, charge is $-2$ on both sides.

hints: Work out the oxidation number of $\text{Cl}$ in $\text{ClO}_2$, in $\text{ClO}_2^-$ and in $\text{ClO}_3^-$, remembering $\text{O}$ is $-2$.
walkthrough:
Define disproportionation in one idea**
Think of one starting species splitting its fate. Disproportionation means the same element in the same starting compound undergoes both oxidation (oxidation number increases) and reduction (oxidation number decreases) at the same time.

Apply it to the chlorine numbers**
In $\text{ClO}_2$, $2 \times (-2) = -4$, so $\text{Cl}$ is $+4$. In $\text{ClO}_2^-$, $\text{Cl}$ is $+3$. In $\text{ClO}_3^-$, $\text{Cl}$ is $+5$. So $+4$ goes up to $+5$ (oxidised) and down to $+3$ (reduced). That is exactly disproportionation.

Final answer: Disproportionation is when the same element is both oxidised and reduced in the same reaction. Here $\text{Cl}$ in $\text{ClO}_2$ (+4) is oxidised to +5 in $\text{ClO}_3^-$ and reduced to +3 in $\text{ClO}_2^-$.

hints: Split the overall equation into two $\text{ClO}_2$ pathways, one forming $\text{ClO}_3^-$ (oxidation, electrons on right) and one forming $\text{ClO}_2^-$ (reduction, electrons on left).
Use $\text{OH}^-$ and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ to balance $\text{O}$ and $\text{H}$ for the oxidation step, remembering the overall equation contains $2\text{OH}^-$ and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$.
walkthrough:
Separate oxidation from reduction**
Sit beside the overall equation: $2\text{ClO}_2 + 2\text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{ClO}_2^- + \text{ClO}_3^- + \text{H}_2\text{O}$. One $\text{ClO}_2$ becomes $\text{ClO}_3^-$. Its $\text{Cl}$ goes $+4$ to $+5$, so it loses one electron. That must be the oxidation half-equation.

Balance the oxidation half-equation**
Write $\text{ClO}_2 \rightarrow \text{ClO}_3^- + \text{e}^-$. You need one extra $\text{O}$ on the left, supplied in alkali by $2\text{OH}^-$, making $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ on the right: $$\text{ClO}_2 + 2\text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{ClO}_3^- + \text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{e}^-$$ Check: $\text{O}$ $4=4$, $\text{H}$ $2=2$, charge $-2 = -2$.

Write the simple reduction half-equation**
The other $\text{ClO}_2$ becomes $\text{ClO}_2^-$. $\text{Cl}$ goes $+4$ to $+3$, so it gains one electron and no $\text{O}$ or $\text{H}$ balancing is needed: $$\text{ClO}_2 + \text{e}^- \rightarrow \text{ClO}_2^-$$ Adding the two half-equations cancels $\text{e}^-$ and gives back the overall equation.

hints: Recall from the Data Booklet the $\text{Li}^+/\text{Li}$ and $\text{I}_2/\text{I}^-$ half-equations, and decide which species loses electrons (lithium oxidised) and which gains electrons (iodine reduced).
To get the overall equation, multiply the lithium half-equation so electrons cancel with the two electrons needed to reduce $\text{I}_2$.
walkthrough:
Assign oxidation and reduction correctly**
You are told lithium is oxidised and iodine is reduced when current flows. Oxidation is loss of electrons, so lithium metal gives $\text{Li}^+$: $$\text{Li} \rightarrow \text{Li}^+ + \text{e}^-$$ Reduction is gain of electrons, so iodine molecules gain electrons to give iodide: $$\text{I}_2 + 2\text{e}^- \rightarrow 2\text{I}^-$$

Combine to cancel electrons**
The iodine half-equation needs $2\text{e}^-$, so you need two lithium atoms to supply them. Multiply the lithium equation by $2$ and add: $$2\text{Li} + \text{I}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{Li}^+ + 2\text{I}^-$$ Electrons cancel exactly, atoms and charge balance.

hints: Pick out $E^\ominus = +0.54\ \text{V}$ for $\text{I}_2/\text{I}^-$ and $E^\ominus = -3.04\ \text{V}$ for $\text{Li}^+/\text{Li}$, then use $E^\ominus_{cell} = E^\ominus_{positive} - E^\ominus_{negative}$.
walkthrough:
Subtract the right way round**
The more positive electrode is iodine ($+0.54\ \text{V}$), the more negative is lithium ($-3.04\ \text{V}$). Standard cell potential is positive minus negative: $$E^\ominus_{cell} = 0.54 - (-3.04) = +3.58\ \text{V}$$ The large positive value tells you the lithium iodine reaction is highly feasible, ideal for a long life pacemaker battery.

hints: Start with moles of lithium used up using $n = m/M_r$ with $M_r(\text{Li}) = 6.9$.
Convert moles of $\text{Li}$ to charge using $Q = n \times F$, where $F = 96500\ \text{C mol}^{-1}$, because each $\text{Li}$ releases one electron.
Rearrange $Q = It$ to $t = Q/I$ and substitute $I = 2.5 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{A}$, remembering $1\ \text{A} = 1\ \text{C s}^{-1}$.
walkthrough:
Find how many moles of electrons must flow**
Only lithium is consumed, and each $\text{Li}$ gives one electron. Moles of $\text{Li}$: $$n(\text{Li}) = \frac{0.10}{6.9} = 1.45 \times 10^{-2}\ \text{mol}$$ So moles of electrons $= 1.45 \times 10^{-2}\ \text{mol}$.

Convert moles of electrons to total charge**
One mole of electrons carries $96500\ \text{C}$ (the Faraday constant). Use $Q = nF$: $$Q = 1.45 \times 10^{-2} \times 96500 = 1399\ \text{C}$$ This is the total charge the $0.10\ \text{g}$ of lithium can deliver.

Convert charge and tiny current to time**
Current is charge per second, $Q = It$, so $t = Q/I$: $$t = \frac{1399}{2.5 \times 10^{-5}} = 5.6 \times 10^{7}\ \text{s}$$ Give at least $2$ significant figures. This huge time, about $1.8$ years, shows why the cell suits a pacemaker drawing only microamps.
